Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette:
Amina is an 80-year-old African American pastor who came to treatment only after months of pressure from her husband and one of the deacons at her church, both of whom had watched her world grow smaller. Decades earlier, before coming to the United States as a refugee, she had been seized during political violence in her home country. She still speaks of that time in fragments. She remembers being forced onto a crowded bus under guard, the metallic clatter of rifles against the bus frame, the sharp commands and cries around her, and the sensation that she was no longer a person with a name but something moved and handled at other people's will. What has stayed with her most is not a coherent story but flashes: the sound of men shouting, the scrape of a weapon, bodies jerking when someone made a sudden move. Even now, when she tries to place the memory in the past, it can feel so extreme that she struggles to believe it truly happened to her.

In the years since, the ordinary settings of her life as a pastor have repeatedly touched those same raw points. Riding the city bus to visit parishioners is especially difficult. The lurch of the vehicle, strangers shifting suddenly in the aisle, and the feeling of being enclosed with no easy exit can make her feel unreal, as if she is no longer fully in her body. Seeing a weapon on a police officer's belt, or even an object held in a way that could be used as a weapon, can stop her in place. In those moments she becomes immediately guarded, watching people's hands and shoulders for any abrupt movement and checking behind her to make sure no one is following. Just as quickly, the old conclusion settles over her that the world is still fundamentally unsafe and that she herself is still living at other people's mercy, never fully restored to ordinary human security. She has come to believe that these reactions prove how unsafe the world remains, and each time they happen she is thrown back into the conviction that what was done to her was profoundly unjust and never answered for.

That sense of injustice sits alongside a more private conviction that if she lets herself think too directly about what happened, she will not be able to bear it. Because of that, she has spent years refusing to speak of the event, even with her husband. When church members ask why she no longer takes the bus across town, she gives practical excuses. She has also developed the habit of dressing in loose, concealing clothing, telling herself she does not want to be noticed. In the hospital clinic she missed two follow-up appointments after becoming distressed in the waiting room, and until now she has avoided psychological care altogether. These choices make sense to her: if she stays covered, says little, and does not put herself in situations that stir things up, she might keep herself together. But over time the very routes she no longer takes and the places she now approaches warily have become reminders in their own right; the bus stop she avoids, the clinic waiting room she dreads, even the need to scan for exits before a church gathering now cue the same anticipatory jolt before anything has actually happened.

Instead, the silence has left the memory with a life of its own. Because she never tells the story through, it forces itself into her mind uninvited, often as sound before image. On the bus she may suddenly hear the shouted commands from years ago as if they are occurring again inside her head. At home, if her husband moves quickly behind her in the kitchen, she startles, scans the room, and a burst of the old scene comes back without warning. The more she stays on guard-eyes on other people, attention fixed on possible danger, repeatedly looking over her shoulder-the more easily the memory breaks through. And when it does, it confirms for her that she is still marked by what happened, still reduced in some fundamental way, "like an object, not a person," as she once said haltingly. Once she has reached that bleak certainty, ordinary details snag more easily on her attention: a crowded aisle, a stranger turning too fast, the outline of something at a person's hip all stand out at once as possible signs that danger is near.

That belief has increasingly shaped where she goes and how she works. As a pastor, she used to travel across the city for hospital visits, prayer meetings, and funerals. Now she rearranges her duties to avoid buses whenever possible, asks others to accompany her, and positions herself near doors during church gatherings. If someone in the congregation makes a sudden movement during a crowded service, she can feel herself go rigid, watching the room instead of listening to the prayer she is meant to lead. Afterwards she is ashamed and angry-angry that the original wrong was never righted, and ashamed that she still feels governed by it. Those thoughts make the next trigger sharper: the detached feeling is enough to frighten her on its own, because she has begun to read it as a sign that she is losing her grip and will not cope if the memory comes fully.

What finally brought Amina in was an incident on a bus she had taken despite herself to visit a sick church elder. A passenger swung a long umbrella while turning, and for an instant it looked like a weapon. She froze, heard shouting in her head, and felt the whole scene become unreal. She got off several stops early and called her husband in tears, something she had never done. She says she is seeking help now because she is afraid that if she continues living this way she will stop being able to serve her church and stop recognizing herself. At the same time, what frightens her most is that speaking about the past may make it all come back with more force than she can survive. Feeling this endangered so suddenly has become, in her own mind, evidence that her life was permanently altered by the violence and that safety is something other people get to take for granted, not her.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers leading to threat and memories, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers directly lead to negative appraisals.
The vignette includes negative appraisals that shape future reactions, but it does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that those appraisals make triggers more likely or more salient.
Although threat and negative appraisals co-occur, no paragraph clearly states that a sense of threat itself leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette describes avoidance and safety behaviours alongside later triggering situations, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves increase or generate triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to threat and memories, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers directly lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette includes negative appraisals that shape future reactions, but it does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that those appraisals make triggers more likely or more salient.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Although threat and negative appraisals co-occur, no paragraph clearly states that a sense of threat itself leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette describes avoidance and safety behaviours alongside later triggering situations, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves increase or generate triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
